Triggers.value: A specific temperature on the skin
A memory of the event coming to mind suddenly

Maladaptive Strategies.value: Paying attention to or looking at my own body
Seeing people that I socialised with before the event
Any form of physical contact with others

Threat.value: I notice potential weapons or dangerous objects in any environment
My body reacts to danger before I have even had time to think
I react with alarm when someone touches me unexpectedly

Negative Appraisals.value: I have to be especially careful because you never know what can happen next
I am permanently an outsider now

issues.item: Avoid Social Contacts: Seeing people that I socialised with before the event
issues.explanation: The social avoidance items are difficult to reconcile with the stated trauma type of childhood physical abuse by a caregiver. These triggers imply avoidance of people linked to a discrete later-life event, but the trauma is chronic/developmental and caregiver-based; there is no corresponding trigger or appraisal content tying prior social contacts or specific intimacy-linked reminders to the abuse history.

issues.item: Avoid Intimacy: Being emotionally close or intimate with others
issues.explanation: Intrusion Monitoring suggests fear of an intruder entering the home, which fits home-invasion or stalking trauma better than childhood caregiver physical abuse. With no accompanying memory or trigger content about nighttime entry, footsteps, doors, or home intrusion, this threat item is hard to explain from the rest of the profile.

issues.item: Intrusion Monitoring: I listen for sounds that might mean someone is entering my home
issues.explanation: No Good Ahead and Outsider are broad, depressive or social-identity appraisals, whereas the other active content is dominated by vigilance, bodily threat detection, and sensory triggering. This combination is not impossible, but here the intimacy/social avoidance items appear to depend on relational shame or alienation that is otherwise underdeveloped and weakly connected to the trigger/threat pattern, reducing coherence.

issues.item: No Good Ahead: Nothing good can happen to me anymore
issues.explanation: Given the formulation, Triggers and Negative Appraisals should be tightly linked, but the chosen triggers are mainly tactile/somatic/intrusive-memory cues while two maladaptive strategies focus on avoiding social contacts and intimacy. Those strategies are not well supported by the trigger set and feel targeted at a different symptom cluster than the one represented elsewhere.

vignette:
Peter is a 66-year-old software engineer who has been married for over forty years, but the architecture of his inner life was laid down decades earlier, in a childhood he rarely speaks about. He grew up with a father whose discipline came unpredictably and violently. He remembers one winter evening in particular: he had left a bicycle in the driveway, and his father yanked him inside by the arm, slammed him onto the cold linoleum floor, and beat him with a leather belt. The details that stay with Peter are not the blows themselves but the sensation of the icy floor against his cheek, the smell of stale beer on his father’s breath, and the frantic pounding of his own heart in his ears. That memory still arrives without warning—often when his skin touches a cold surface, or when his heart starts racing from even mild exertion. Each time, his body reacts before his mind has a chance to catch up: his muscles lock, his breath shortens, and he feels an urgent need to scan the room for anything that could be used as a weapon. The startle response has become so ingrained that when a colleague claps him on the shoulder in greeting, Peter jerks away, his pulse already hammering.

These episodes reinforce a conviction that has taken root over a lifetime: people cannot be trusted, and he is permanently an outsider. Peter believes that if he lets his guard down for a moment, danger will find him. Once he had concluded that people could not be trusted, ordinary cues began to feel like warnings—a colleague pausing in the hallway, the unexpected ring of a phone, the jingle of keys in a pocket—each one demanding his eyes dart toward it before his mind could decide whether it mattered. This constant vigilance colors his every interaction. At work, he keeps his desk turned so that he can see the door; in meetings, he notices the sharp corner of a letter opener or the weight of a paperweight. He has come to view his own body as a liability—its reactions betray him, and he avoids paying attention to it whenever possible. When he catches a glimpse of himself in the mirror, he looks away, unsettled by the vulnerability he sees. He has also withdrawn from the small circle of friends he once had, convinced that no one could understand what he carries, and that socializing is simply an invitation to be caught off guard. His wife has learned not to touch him from behind, but even her hand on his arm in the kitchen can trigger a flinch. He does not like the way his body feels under her touch; it reminds him of the cold floor, of being pinned down, of his own helplessness.

Over the years, Peter’s avoidance has deepened the very beliefs it was meant to manage. By steering clear of others, he confirms his sense of being apart. By not looking at his body, he avoids confronting the shame and fragility he associates with it—but the heart still pounds, and the cold still prickles, and each physical sensation becomes another proof that danger is imminent. He has noticed that the more he tries to ignore his bodily signals, the more they intrude. His heart races on a quiet walk; the cold of a glass of water brings the memory crashing back. And each time, the world feels a little more threatening, and he retreats a little further. He is exhausted by the effort of staying on guard. That unrelenting hum of threat made anything with a sharp edge or a sudden sound into a potential signal—the scrape of a chair leg, a car door slamming outside, even the way a coat hung on a hook could catch his attention and hold it until he forced himself to look away. What finally brought him to seek help was a moment last month when he found himself staring at a pair of scissors on his desk, his breath shallow, his fists clenched, unable to remember how long he had been frozen there. He is afraid that one day he will not be able to pull himself back, and that the outsider he feels himself to be will become permanently locked inside his own body.

violations.explanation: The vignette does not show that Peter's negative appraisals (e.g., distrust, feeling like an outsider) cause him to experience triggering stimuli; instead, triggers lead to appraisals.
The vignette does not depict that Peter's sense of threat causes new triggers; rather, triggers lead to threat and avoidance.

vignette_attempts.feedback:
REQUIRED EDGES MISSING:
- Negative Appraisals → Triggers: The vignette does not show that Peter's negative appraisals (e.g., distrust, feeling like an outsider) cause him to experience triggering stimuli; instead, triggers lead to appraisals.
  e.g. "Once she had concluded that the world was fundamentally unsafe, almost anything could confirm it — a figure in her periphery, the wrong tone of voice, footsteps behind her."
  e.g. "The belief that she couldn't trust her own judgement meant that things she would once have registered and dismissed now snagged and held her attention."
  e.g. "Her conviction that it would happen again meant she moved through ordinary days as if they were mined — every ambiguity became a potential signal."
- Threat → Triggers: The vignette does not depict that Peter's sense of threat causes new triggers; rather, triggers lead to threat and avoidance.
  e.g. "Already running on threat, she found that almost anything could tip into a warning — a van parked at an odd angle, a light left on that shouldn't have been."
  e.g. "The background hum of danger she carried everywhere made ordinary cues feel like messages — each one confirming what her body already believed."
  e.g. "Living at that pitch of alertness, she found the world had become dense with reminders she couldn't stop reading."
